analysis.one_liner: Lets Medicare negotiate prescription drug prices directly with drug manufacturers.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing, markup, or vote, after being referred there the same day it was introduced.
analysis.plain_summary: When Medicare's prescription drug benefit was created in 2003, Congress wrote in a "non-interference" clause that barred the government from negotiating drug prices or requiring plans to use a set price list. This bill would repeal that ban and let the Secretary of Health and Human Services negotiate with drug manufacturers, the way other federal agencies that buy drugs in bulk already do. The stated goal was to make sure every Medicare enrollee pays the lowest possible price for covered drugs. [S2] [S3]
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who pay out-of-pocket costs and premiums tied to drug prices. If the government could negotiate lower prices the way the VA and other federal purchasers do, seniors' drug costs and Medicare's part of the bill would fall, and taxpayers would save on the federal share of the drug benefit. [S2] [S3]

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the 'non-interference' provision that forbids the Secretary of Health and Human Services from interfering in negotiations between drug manufacturers, pharmacies, and drug plans, or from requiring a plan formulary to use a set reimbursement price structure.

Gives the Secretary authority similar to that of other federal agencies that buy prescription drugs in bulk — such as those using VA-style purchasing — to negotiate contracts with manufacturers of drugs covered under Medicare Part D, in order to secure the lowest possible price for enrollees.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, whose revenues depend on Medicare paying market prices set through private plan negotiations rather than government-negotiated contracts. If negotiated prices cut into manufacturers' profits, the industry argues this could mean less money available for developing new drugs.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not say how the Secretary's negotiated prices would flow down to what individual seniors actually pay at the pharmacy, since Part D coverage would continue to run through private plans; the mechanism's real-world savings depend entirely on how negotiation is carried out.

Drug manufacturers and their allies argued that government negotiation amounts to price controls that would reduce industry revenue and, over time, the investment in new medicines — a trade-off any honest supporter would have to weigh against lower costs for seniors.

Private drug plans and pharmacy benefit managers already negotiate prices on behalf of enrollees, and critics contended that government bargaining would duplicate or displace that role rather than add savings on top of it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly tens of millions of Medicare beneficiaries, the potential upside is large: drug prices negotiated on behalf of the single biggest purchaser of prescription drugs in the country, with savings shared by seniors and taxpayers. The main honest cost is to the pharmaceutical industry's revenue, and the industry's argument that lower prices mean less drug development is real but speculative — the same argument has been made against every federal bulk-purchasing program, including the VA's. The bill's chief design weakness is that it authorizes negotiation without specifying how negotiated prices reach enrollees through private plans.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the same day, and no further action was ever taken on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on February 17, 2005 by Sen. Debbie Stabenow, with Sens. Carper, Kennedy, Schumer, Bingaman, and Johnson joining as original sponsors.
On the day it was introduced, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance.
The full action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action — the bill sat in committee until the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.
Because the bill died, the 2003 ban on Medicare negotiating drug prices remained in place throughout the 109th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers came out ahead: by keeping the bill bottled up in committee, the industry preserved the statutory ban on Medicare price negotiation and continued to sell to Medicare beneficiaries at privately negotiated prices. Private Part D drug plans also kept their role as the sole negotiating channel.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers and private drug plans

for.name: Sen. Debbie Stabenow
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to allow Medicare drug price negotiation and spoke in support of it on the Senate floor.

for.name: 11 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsors Carper, Kennedy, Schumer, Bingaman, and Johnson.

against.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee the bill was referred to, never scheduled a hearing or markup; the action history shows no committee activity after referral.

against.name: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA)
against.what_they_did: Fought to preserve the ban on government drug price negotiation that the industry had secured in the 2003 Medicare drug law, and opposed legislation allowing Medicare to negotiate prices.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 11 cosponsors were Democrats; with Republicans in control of the Senate and its Finance Committee, the bill never advanced past referral.

industries.note: The bill would replace the current setup — where prices emerge from private plan negotiations and the government is barred from interfering — with government-negotiated contracts. The industry's revenue from Medicare, its largest customer segment, depends on keeping the ban in place, so its interest ran directly against seniors seeking lower drug prices.

industries.industry: Private Part D drug plan sponsors and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: The bill leaves the drug benefit itself inside private plans, keeping insurers and PBMs as the ongoing administrators of coverage, while adding a government negotiating layer on top. Their administrative role is preserved, but a strong government negotiator could shrink the margin they earn on drug pricing.
